doc.title: Roland Hanna interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

title: Letting the music develop itself; Alvin Batiste
summary: Rowe praises a composer's sense in his solo; Hanna describes letting music flow and mentions Alvin Batiste.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I have to say listening to one particular solo you played today, that you really have what I consider to be a composer’s sense in your improvising. There’s a great use of a mixture of chording, rhythmic things, and you did something just in octaves, you know, one octave delayed off the other, and I mean it’s a great device.

I try to use material that sort of either — I can’t say needs development — but develops itself. I try to let the music develop itself. That’s what I try to do. When I make a conscious effort at it it doesn’t work. But when I make a feeling effort, in other words when I let the music flow out, then it works. And whatever I have to do to get it out, it’s not so much that I’m forcing the physical part, the physical part happens. Like sometimes I can hear repeated notes. Fortunately for me I had teachers who taught me how to play repeated notes. Because otherwise I’d be trying to do it with my wrist and you can’t do that. But they showed me how you do it with your fingers. You just do it. So now I’m practicing enough so that it’s natural. And those things come out, not because they’re technical but because it’s part of the way I hear now. I was talking to Brunious a while ago about Alvin Batiste. And Alvin Batiste is one of those people who hears a certain way. And having studied his clarinet so much, he does things very naturally. I don’t know whether you know him, if you do know him you might know what I mean. When he plays he plays an angular kind of pattern that shift back and forth before you know it, and he’s playing on regular harmonies, but it’s very unusual sounding. Well that’s what happens sometimes when I play. It develops, but I never know how it’s going to develop. Never know. It just happens on its own. Well thanks for thinking of that.
